newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU pressing Washington to abolish 1916 trade act.
newsitem.headline: EU pressing Washington to abolish 1916 trade act.

text.p: The European Commission is pressing Washington to dismantle decades-old U.S. trade legislation recently used against a Germany steel producer, officials said on Wednesday.

Confirming the Commission had receieved a complaint from EUROFER -- the trade association of European iron and steel producers -- an official said it had already raised the question of the private Antidumping Act of 1916 with Washington.
"Our understanding is that the U.S. was scheduled to abolish this law during the current congress," the official said. "It is an antiquated piece of legislation that has no place today."

EUROFER said on Wednesday it had petitioned the Commission to launch a complaint in response to a suit filed under the act in Utah in September by U.S. company Geneva Steel Corp. against Germany's Thyssen Steel Group and others.

Geneva Steel is seeking $90 million in damages from Thyssen and Houston-based importer Ranger Steel Supply Corp, accusing them of attempting to undermine the U.S. industry by selling underpriced plate imports from China, Russia and Ukraine.

The 1916 Private Antidumping Act allows American individuals or companies to press for material damages or jail sentences against companies they accuse of deliberately attempting to harm markets by underpricing goods.
Trade lawyers say the law is rarely used and a suit has never been successfully filed.

In response to a complaint by Geneva Steel, the U.S. International Trade Commission said on December 18 that it had found "reasonable indication" American markets were being hurt by imported steel plate from these countries.
The ITC is due to release a final report on April 14 and the investigation could eventually lead to anti-dumping duties being imposed.
In its petition to the European Commission, EUROFER said it had identified "seven critical areas in which the 1916 Act contravenes World Trade Organisation (WTO) rules.

Under EU procedures, the Commission must decide within 45 days whether to launch a formal investigation into EUROFER's complaint. An investigation could take up to five months and lead to a dispute being lodged with the WTO.
